title: Eight Weeks of Taking Your Questions Seriously
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for the person taking apart an inherited faith: sort what you were handed, face the hard questions, and dig for what is older, with no panic and no ambush.
intro:
This is an eight week walk for the person taking apart the faith they were handed, piece by piece, to see what will hold. Nobody here will panic about that. Looking hard at what you were given isn't a sin, and some of it deserves to go. But the church culture you were raised in is not the same thing as the faith Christians have confessed for centuries, and you can lose the first without losing the second. Each week holds one focus, one small practice, one thing to read, one tool, and one honest question. The weeks move from sorting what you're actually questioning, through the hard texts and the church's failures, down to the older faith underneath, and they end in company. The aim is not to talk you out of anything or into anything. It is to make sure that whatever you decide, you decide about the real thing.

It isn't a cure, and it isn't a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, or the real people who can walk with you. If someone at home threatens you or uses God to control you, call the Domestic Violence Hotline listed on Find Help before you go any further. If a church leader abused you, that is more than deconstruction, and the care page linked in week four is for you first. Walk the plan imperfectly. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up. Nobody is timing you, and nobody is waiting at week eight with an altar call. You're allowed to take years.
careNote: If the heaviness has spread into your sleep, appetite, work, or closest relationships for two weeks or more, or a fear of hell keeps coming back, see a doctor or a licensed counselor, one who has worked with people hurt in a church if that is part of your story. In a crisis, call or text 988, and if anyone is in danger now, call 911.

weeks.focus: Naming what you are actually questioning
weeks.why: God and Jesus, the Bible, the church and its leaders, politics and culture, and the rules you were raised with are different things, but most of us were handed them as one package. Pastors like me hand that package over, and we haven't always marked which pieces were essential and which were extras. So when one piece fails, everything shakes, and it can feel as if all of it is falling at once. Usually it isn't. The first work is sorting, not deciding.
weeks.practice: Each day, write one line naming something you no longer believe or aren't sure of. Then mark where it belongs: God and Jesus, the Bible, the church and its leaders, politics and culture, or the rules you were raised with. Don't argue with any of it yet. If one pile grows faster than the others, that shows you where the real work is.

read.label: I'm deconstructing my faith: the care page this plan walks more slowly

tool.label: When It All Comes Apart, a five-session study whose first session asks what you are actually taking apart

weeks.reflection: When I say I am losing my faith, which faith do I mean, and who taught it to me?

weeks.focus: Separating Jesus from the version you were handed
weeks.why: Every generation drapes something over the text. For some of us the Jesus we inherited came wrapped in a flag, for others in a cause, and either way he was sanded smooth where he is sharp and sharpened where he is gentle. That is how some people take apart a faith fused to one party and rebuild, almost without noticing, a faith fused to the other. Before you decide about him, it's worth meeting the one on the page. He is stranger than the one you were sold.
weeks.practice: Read a chapter or two of the Gospel of Mark each day, as if for the first time. Write down each place where the Jesus on the page differs from the one you were handed, and keep the list.

read.label: Mark 1 in the Study Bible, the shortest Gospel from its first line, with notes on every chapter

tool.label: Which Lens Has You? Thirteen honest choices that name the flag, the cause, and the other lenses that read for us

weeks.reflection: How much of what I am rejecting did Jesus actually say, and how much was added by the people who taught me?

weeks.focus: The hard texts, faced instead of dodged
weeks.why: Some of what you're questioning isn't the church at all. It's the book: the conquest chapters, the slavery laws, the passages your old church skipped on the way to the encouraging parts. They are in the Bible, and the person who refuses to look away is reading more honestly than the one who skips them. You were probably taught to manage these texts rather than face them. This week you face them slowly and in their setting, with notes that state the hard question plainly and give more than one honest answer.
weeks.practice: Choose the passage that troubles you most and read it slowly, in full and in its setting, a little each day. Read the chapter's notes too, including the hard question where there is one. Write down what the notes resolved for you and what they honestly did not.

read.label: Deuteronomy 20 in the Study Bible, where the hard question on the conquest gets several honest answers

tool.label: The Study Bible, to find the passage that troubles you most, with notes on every chapter

weeks.reflection: Which text have I been carrying as a private objection for years, and have I ever actually read it in full?

weeks.focus: What the church got wrong, said plainly
weeks.why: Some of what you're leaving deserves to be left. Churches have protected a leader's name instead of the people he hurt, fused the faith to a flag or a cause, taught shame and called it holiness, and sold a certainty they did not own. I'm a pastor, and I don't get to say this from a safe distance, because people like me built some of it. Naming it accurately is not bitterness. It's the beginning of telling the truth, and nothing real gets rebuilt on a lie. If what happened to you was abuse, that is more than deconstruction. Report any crime, and any harm to a child, to the police. If someone at home threatens you or uses God to control you, call the Domestic Violence Hotline on Find Help, and don't agree to couples counseling with someone who frightens you.
weeks.practice: Write a letter you will not send, naming what the church did to you or near you, a few lines each day. Use plain words, with no softening and no exaggerating, because accuracy is the discipline. Keep it with your week one list. If the writing brings up abuse or a crime, stop and reach for safety and help first, and let the letter wait.

read.label: The church hurt me: the care page for anyone wounded by a church or the people who led it

tool.label: Find Help, where the hotlines are listed, because if what was done to you was abuse you need doors, not essays

weeks.reflection: What did the church actually cost me, and can I say it without making it smaller or larger than it was?

weeks.focus: What you would be leaving, and what you would be keeping
weeks.why: Taking apart is easier than building, and it can become a place to live. Wholesale exit feels clean, but somewhere in the package there may be things that are yours, things you would grieve, things that were true even when the people teaching them were not. Scripture shows another way to take a faith apart. When the Book of the Law was found in the temple, King Josiah tore down what had been added and recovered what was older (2 Kings 22 and 23). An inventory is not a commitment. It's a map of what is actually at stake, made before the decision instead of after.
weeks.practice: Keep two running lists this week, one of what you would gladly leave and one of what you would grieve losing. Add at least one item to either list each day, and be specific: names, practices, claims.

read.label: 2 Kings 22 in the Study Bible, Josiah and the book found in the temple

tool.label: 1 Corinthians 3 in the Study Bible, on the builders, the straw, and the one foundation

weeks.reflection: If I left tomorrow, what would I miss that is actually about God and not just about belonging?

weeks.focus: The strongest case against, and the strongest case for
weeks.why: A faith examined only by its defenders has not been examined, and a faith examined only by its critics has not been examined either. You were probably taught to fear the strongest objections, and fear is not an argument. Neither is resentment. This week you build both cases at full strength, starting at the center, which is a claim about an event: that a crucified man was raised on the third day. A verdict reached against a straw man is not a verdict.
weeks.practice: Each day, write a paragraph of the best case against what you were taught, at full strength and with no straw, and then a paragraph of the best case for it, the same way. By the week's end you should have one honest page of each, side by side.

read.label: Luke 24 in the Study Bible, where the hard question on the resurrection states the skeptics' case first

tool.label: Did the Gospels Get Jesus Right? The telephone-game objection stated at full strength before it is answered

weeks.reflection: Have I ever heard the strongest version of the other side from someone who actually holds it?

weeks.why: Rebuilding is not the same as writing a faith of your own, and swapping old certainties for new ones only builds the same house in a different color. What lies under the package is smaller than the package, and older. When Paul summed up what he had passed on, it fit in a sentence: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). The creeds that grew from that confession say nothing about a party or a dating rule, and they ask you to believe more, not less. Writing to a church split into camps, Paul put it plainly: "no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 3:11).
weeks.practice: Read the Apostles' Creed slowly, a few lines a day, and mark each line with one of three notes: I believe this, I'm not sure, or I don't. Notice what isn't there. Before the week ends, choose one thing Jesus says to do in the Sermon on the Mount and do it, because some of what you're looking for is found by doing.

read.label: The Apostles' Creed, the full text with plain notes, to mark line by line

tool.label: Matthew 5 in the Study Bible, the start of the Sermon on the Mount, to find one thing Jesus said and do it

weeks.reflection: Which line of the creed can I say honestly today, and which am I not ready to say?

weeks.why: The worst decisions about faith are made alone and fast, in either direction, so there is no deadline on this one. When many of his followers walked away, Jesus asked the Twelve, "Do you want to leave too?" (John 6:67), and he let them answer. Peter answered with a question of his own: "Lord, to whom would we go?" (John 6:68). Before you set Jesus down with everything else, ask Peter's question honestly, and ask it in company. Whatever you decide, decide it as a person who has been heard, not as a person who finally snapped in private. You're allowed to take years.
weeks.practice: Choose one person who won't panic or cheer: a pastor from outside your old church, a friend who believes and can bear your questions, or a counselor. Each day, add a line to what you want them to know, and before the week ends, show them your lists and the creed you marked. Think twice before narrating it all online. If you can pray at all, borrow older words and read Psalm 42 aloud, slowly.

read.label: John 6 in the Study Bible, where many walked away and Jesus let the Twelve answer

tool.label: Psalm 42 in the Study Bible, borrowed words for someone who can't sing the old songs today

weeks.reflection: Who can hear where I actually am without needing me to land somewhere, and when will I talk with them?
